title: Module Overview and Imports
content: The file imports three Mathlib modules: `GroupTheory.Solvable` (definition of `IsSolvable` and the derived series), `GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Alternating` (the proof that $A_5$ is simple via `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`), and `Tactic` (general-purpose tactics). The module documents the 4-step proof chain from $A_5$ simplicity to Abel-Ruffini and connects to two sibling files in the gallery: `AbelRuffini.lean` (base theorem via `solvableByRad`) and `AbelRuffiniGaloisExtensions.lean` (solvability classifications). This is part of Wiedijk's "100 Theorems" project (#16, Insolvability of General Higher Degree Equations).
mathContext: The file formalizes the proof chain: $A_5$ simple $\Rightarrow$ $S_n$ ($n \geq 5$) not solvable $\Rightarrow$ no radical formula for the general quintic. All group-theoretic content comes from Mathlib's `GroupTheory` library.

title: Part I Header and Proof Architecture
content:
The file is organized into a single namespace `AbelRuffiniOQ04` with five clearly separated parts, mirroring the logical structure of the Abel-Ruffini proof chain. Part I establishes the foundation (A₅ simplicity), Part II builds the main non-solvability theorem, Part III provides contrast cases, Part IV packages the threshold result, and Part V provides comprehensive documentation. This 'OQ-04' designation indicates the fourth original question/exploration branching from the base `abel-ruffini` gallery entry, focusing specifically on making the internal proof chain explicit.

**Design choice:** The modular architecture ensures that each link in the chain can be independently verified and reused. For instance, `symmetric_not_solvable` can be imported directly by any downstream proof about polynomial solvability without pulling in the pedagogical documentation. In Lean 4's type-theoretic foundation, each theorem is a term whose type is its statement — `a5_is_simple` has type `IsSimpleGroup (alternatingGroup (Fin 5))`, and `symmetric_not_solvable` has type `(n : ℕ) → 5 ≤ n → ¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`. Naming each step makes these types individually accessible as API surface, enabling composability with other formalizations.
mathContext: The proof chain architecture: foundation ($A_5$ simple) $\to$ propagation ($S_n$ not solvable) $\to$ contrast ($S_{\leq 4}$ solvable) $\to$ threshold (exact dichotomy) $\to$ documentation (full chain).

title: A₅ Is Simple — The Foundation
content:
The cornerstone of the entire chain: the alternating group A₅ is simple (has no proper non-trivial normal subgroups). This is the deepest fact used, proved in Mathlib by explicit computation on permutations. A₅ is the smallest non-abelian simple group, with order |A₅| = 60 = 5!/2. Its simplicity is equivalent to saying that the only normal subgroups are {e} and A₅ itself. The complete list of simple groups (the Classification of Finite Simple Groups) shows that A₅ ≅ PSL(2,4) ≅ PSL(2,5) is the first in the infinite family of alternating simple groups.

**Why A₅ is simple (standard proof):** The conjugacy classes of A₅ have sizes 1, 12, 12, 15, 20. Any normal subgroup must be a union of conjugacy classes including {e}, and its order must divide 60. The only sub-sums of {1, 12, 12, 15, 20} that include 1 and divide 60 are 1 and 60 — so the only normal subgroups are {e} and A₅.

**Burnside context:** Note that |A₅| = 60 = 2² · 3 · 5 involves three distinct primes. By Burnside's p^a q^b theorem (1904), every group of order p^a q^b (two primes) is solvable. A₅ is the smallest group escaping this criterion, making it the minimal counterexample to solvability in a precise sense.

**Feit-Thompson connection:** The Feit-Thompson odd-order theorem (1963) proves that every finite group of odd order is solvable — a 255-page proof that earned Thompson the Fields Medal (1970). This means any non-solvable finite group must have even order. Since |A₅| = 60 is even, this is consistent — but the theorem explains *why* the search for a non-solvable group inevitably leads to even-order groups. Combined with Burnside's theorem, the constraints tighten: A₅ must have order divisible by at least three distinct primes and be even, and 60 = 2²·3·5 is the smallest such number admitting a simple group.

**Geometric incarnation:** A₅ ≅ the rotation group of the regular icosahedron (and its dual, the regular dodecahedron). The 60 rotational symmetries — 1 identity, 24 face rotations (72° and 144° around 6 axes), 20 vertex rotations (120° and 240° around 10 axes), and 15 edge rotations (180° around 15 axes) — correspond exactly to the 60 even permutations in A₅. Klein (1884) exploited this isomorphism to solve the general quintic via the icosahedral equation, showing that while no radical formula exists (Abel-Ruffini), the quintic IS solvable using functions adapted to icosahedral symmetry.

**Character-theoretic proof:** An alternative route to A₅ simplicity uses representation theory. A₅ has exactly 5 conjugacy classes (sizes 1, 12, 12, 15, 20), giving a 5×5 character table with irreducible representations of dimensions 1, 3, 3, 4, 5 (satisfying 1² + 3² + 3² + 4² + 5² = 60 = |A₅|). A normal subgroup must be a union of conjugacy classes and a kernel of some character — but inspecting the character table shows the only characters with kernel larger than {e} are trivial. This representation-theoretic approach generalizes: character theory is a primary tool in the Classification of Finite Simple Groups.

**Exceptional isomorphisms:** A₅ exhibits a remarkable triple coincidence with the projective special linear groups: A₅ ≅ PSL₂(𝔽₄) ≅ PSL₂(𝔽₅). The isomorphism A₅ ≅ PSL₂(𝔽₅) arises because PSL₂(𝔽₅) acts on the 6 points of the projective line ℙ¹(𝔽₅), but the conjugation action on the 5 Sylow 2-subgroups gives a transitive action on 5 elements (giving the embedding into A₅; equality follows by orders, |PSL₂(𝔽₅)| = (5²-1)(5²-5)/(2·4) = 60 = |A₅|). The isomorphism A₅ ≅ PSL₂(𝔽₄) comes from |PSL₂(𝔽₄)| = (4²-1)(4²-4)/(1·3) = 60 — note PSL₂(𝔽₄) = SL₂(𝔽₄) since 𝔽₄ has characteristic 2. These coincidences are unique to order 60: for q ≥ 7, PSL₂(𝔽_q) and A_n diverge, with each PSL₂(𝔽_q) becoming a distinct simple group in the infinite Lie-type family.

**Inverse Galois problem:** Hilbert (1892) proved that A₅ is realizable as a Galois group over ℚ — that is, there exists a Galois extension K/ℚ with Gal(K/ℚ) ≅ A₅. One concrete witness is the splitting field of $x^5 - x - 1$, whose discriminant is $2869 = 19 \cdot 151$ (not a perfect square), giving Galois group $S_5$; for $A_5$-realization, polynomials with square discriminant such as $x^5 + 20x + 16$ work. Hilbert's proof uses his irreducibility theorem: a polynomial irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ remains irreducible after specializing $t$ to infinitely many rationals. Shafarevich (1954) extended Hilbert's result to all solvable groups, but realizability of every finite simple group over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a major open problem in the inverse Galois conjecture. Note the asymmetry: Abel-Ruffini's *negative* result (no radical formula for the generic quintic) and the *positive* realizability of $A_5$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ are about different questions — the first about expressibility of roots, the second about which groups appear as symmetry groups.
mathContext: $A_5$ is simple: the only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$. $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$. By the Jordan-Hölder theorem, $A_5$ appears as the unique composition factor (up to isomorphism) in any composition series of $S_5$ that passes through $A_5$. Character-theoretic proof: irreducible representations have dimensions $1, 3, 3, 4, 5$ with $1^2 + 3^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 = 60$. Exceptional isomorphisms: $A_5 \cong \text{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4) \cong \text{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$, all of order 60. Realizable as $\text{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ for $K$ the splitting field of an irreducible quintic with square discriminant (Hilbert 1892).

title: Part II: Propagating Non-Solvability to Symmetric Groups
content:
Part II takes the A₅ simplicity established in Part I and propagates it upward: since A₅ is non-solvable and A₅ embeds into Aₙ for all n ≥ 5, and Aₙ is a normal subgroup of Sₙ, the entire symmetric group Sₙ is forced to be non-solvable. This is the step that converts a fact about one specific group (A₅) into a universal statement about all large symmetric groups.

**Propagation mechanism:** The key group-theoretic fact is that solvability is inherited by subgroups: if G is solvable, so is every subgroup H ≤ G (since the derived series of H is contained in the derived series of G restricted to H). Contrapositively: if H ≤ G is not solvable, neither is G. The embedding A₅ ↪ Aₙ ≤ Sₙ makes Sₙ inherit non-solvability from A₅.
mathContext: $A_5 \hookrightarrow A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ for $n \geq 5$. Non-solvability propagates: $A_5$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ $A_n$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ $S_n$ not solvable.

title: Sₙ Not Solvable for n ≥ 5
content: The main theorem: the symmetric group Sₙ is not solvable for n ≥ 5. The proof uses Mathlib's Equiv.Perm.not_solvable, which internally works via the chain: A₅ is simple and non-abelian → A₅ is not solvable → Aₙ contains A₅ for n ≥ 5 → Aₙ is not solvable → Sₙ is not solvable (since quotients of solvable groups are solvable, but Sₙ/Aₙ ≅ ℤ/2ℤ would make Aₙ solvable if Sₙ were). The main technical contribution of this file is bridging a type mismatch between the natural number hypothesis and Mathlib's cardinal-level statement. The proof proceeds in two steps: (1) `simp only [Cardinal.mk_fintype, Fintype.card_fin]` rewrites the goal from `5 ≤ Cardinal.mk (Fin n)` to `5 ≤ ↑(Fintype.card (Fin n))` and then to `5 ≤ ↑n`, reducing the cardinal expression to a coercion of the natural number n into `Cardinal`; (2) `exact_mod_cast hn` discharges the resulting `5 ≤ ↑n` by recognizing that the hypothesis `hn : 5 ≤ n` in ℕ lifts to the coerced cardinal inequality via `Nat.cast_le`. This two-line bridge is the file's only new proof content — everything else delegates to Mathlib.
mathContext: For $n \geq 5$: $A_5 \hookrightarrow A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$. If $S_n$ were solvable, so would $A_n$ (as a subgroup), hence $A_5$ — contradicting its non-solvability. Therefore $S_n$ is not solvable.

title: Specific Non-Solvable Cases: S₅, S₆, S₇
content:
Instantiates symmetric_not_solvable for n = 5, 6, 7, giving directly usable theorems. S₅ uses le_rfl (5 ≤ 5 by reflexivity), while S₆ and S₇ use omega (Lean's arithmetic decision procedure for linear arithmetic over ℕ and ℤ). These named instances make it easy to apply the non-solvability results in downstream proofs about specific polynomial degrees — for instance, s5_not_solvable is precisely the fact needed to conclude that the generic quintic has no radical formula, while s6_not_solvable and s7_not_solvable extend this to sextic and septic polynomials.

**The exceptional case S₆:** Among all symmetric groups Sₙ (n ≥ 3), S₆ is uniquely distinguished by having an outer automorphism: |Out(S₆)| = 2, while |Out(Sₙ)| = 1 for all other n ≥ 3. This exceptional outer automorphism — discovered by Sylvester (1844) and connected to the exceptional isomorphism PSL(2,9) ≅ A₆ — swaps the conjugacy classes of transpositions and products of three disjoint transpositions. Despite this richer internal structure, S₆ is no more solvable than S₅: the obstruction (A₅ ⊂ A₆) is invariant under outer automorphisms, since any automorphism preserves the derived series and hence solvability. The existence of the outer automorphism is a combinatorial accident: it arises because S₆ has exactly 6 Sylow 5-subgroups, allowing S₆ to act on them by conjugation and giving a non-inner embedding S₆ → S₆.

**Connection to Hilbert's 13th:** The s7_not_solvable instance connects directly to Hilbert's 13th problem (1900), which asked whether degree-7 polynomial roots require genuinely trivariate functions. Abel-Ruffini rules out radicals (univariate operations), but the question of minimal variable count remained open until Kolmogorov and Arnold (1957) showed that continuous functions of any number of variables decompose into functions of one variable — resolving Hilbert's question in the continuous category, though the algebraic version remains subtle.
mathContext: $S_5, S_6, S_7$ are all non-solvable, obtained by specializing $\forall n \geq 5,\ \neg\text{IsSolvable}(S_n)$. Proof terms: `le_rfl` for $5 \leq 5$ (reflexivity), `omega` for $5 \leq 6$ and $5 \leq 7$ (linear arithmetic decision procedure over $\mathbb{N}$).

title: Part III: The Solvable Side — Contrast Cases
content:
Part III provides the other side of the dichotomy: small symmetric groups ARE solvable. This section exists for pedagogical completeness — without knowing that S₀ through S₄ are solvable, the non-solvability of S₅ lacks context. The contrast makes the threshold at degree 5 visually and conceptually sharp: we see exactly where the boundary lies.

**Why S₄ is the last solvable case:** The key structural difference is that A₄ has the Klein four-group V₄ = {e, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)} as a normal subgroup, while A₅ has no proper non-trivial normal subgroup. V₄ allows the derived series of S₄ to descend: S₄ ⊵ A₄ ⊵ V₄ ⊵ {e}. In A₅, there is no such 'stepping stone' — the derived series immediately gets stuck.
mathContext: Contrast: $S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$ are all solvable. The transition $S_4 \to S_5$ is the exact break point, driven by $A_5$ being the first non-abelian simple group.

title: Small Symmetric Groups Are Solvable
content:
Demonstrates that S₀ and S₁ are solvable via Lean's inferInstance, which finds the solvability proof automatically from Mathlib's typeclass instances. These trivial cases (S₀ ≅ {e}, S₁ ≅ {e}) contrast with the non-solvable cases above. The full picture is: S₀ through S₄ are solvable, while S₅ onward are not. S₂ ≅ ℤ/2ℤ (abelian), S₃ ≅ D₃ (derived series {e} ◁ A₃ ◁ S₃), and S₄ has derived series {e} ◁ V₄ ◁ A₄ ◁ S₄ where V₄ is the Klein four-group.

**Why only S₀ and S₁?** Mathlib's typeclass system also provides `IsSolvable` instances for S₂, S₃, and S₄ (all can be proved by `inferInstance`), but the file shows only two contrast cases for minimality. The pedagogical choice is deliberate: S₀ and S₁ are the simplest possible witnesses that solvability exists, and together with `five_is_the_threshold` in Part IV, they bracket the full solvable range without enumerating every case. Proving all five cases (S₀–S₄) would add completeness at the cost of redundancy, since the file's focus is the *non-solvability* chain rather than a complete classification. The companion gallery entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02` ("S₂, S₃, S₄ Are Solvable: Complete Classification") fills this gap with explicit derived series arguments for each of S₂, S₃, and S₄ — and goes further, establishing the bidirectional theorem: $S_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. That entry makes the degree-by-degree derived series table in Part V fully machine-checked, with each composition factor verified independently.

**Smallest non-abelian vs. smallest non-abelian simple:** S₃ (order 6) is the smallest non-abelian group, yet it IS solvable — its derived series {e} ◁ A₃ ◁ S₃ terminates because A₃ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ is abelian. The crucial distinction is between 'non-abelian' (compatible with solvability via a subnormal series with abelian factors) and 'non-abelian simple' (which blocks solvability entirely, since [G,G] = G for simple non-abelian G). A₅ (order 60) is the smallest non-abelian simple group — 10 times larger than S₃. This gap reflects how much internal structure a group must accumulate before it can resist all decomposition into abelian factors. The analogy to polynomial solvability is precise: the cubic's Galois group (≤ S₃) is always solvable, giving Cardano's formula; the quintic's Galois group can be S₅ ⊃ A₅, which is not solvable, blocking radical formulas.
mathContext: $S_0 \cong S_1 \cong \{e\}$ are trivially solvable. The complete picture: $S_n$ is solvable $\iff n \leq 4$. Derived series: $S_2$: $\{e\} \triangleleft S_2$; $S_3$: $\{e\} \triangleleft A_3 \triangleleft S_3$ (with $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$); $S_4$: $\{e\} \triangleleft V_4 \triangleleft A_4 \triangleleft S_4$ where $V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$ is the Klein four-group.

title: Part IV: Packaging the Sharp Dichotomy
content:
Part IV distills the results of Parts II and III into a single theorem witnessing the solvability threshold. Where Part II proved non-solvability for n ≥ 5 and Part III showed solvability for small n, Part IV packages these into a conjunction that formally locates the phase transition. This step is mathematically trivial but pedagogically essential: it makes the sharp dichotomy at n = 5 a single quotable result rather than a pair of separate theorems scattered across the file.

**Mathematical significance of the exact threshold:** The transition at n = 5 is not just a curiosity — it explains why the historical search for a quintic formula was doomed. Lagrange's approach (1771) of analyzing resolvents worked for degrees ≤ 4 precisely because S₄ is solvable: each quotient in the derived series corresponds to a radical extraction step. At degree 5, Lagrange's method produces a resolvent of degree 6 rather than reducing the degree — a symptom of the non-solvability that Abel and Galois would later prove.
mathContext: The solvability threshold theorem: $\text{IsSolvable}(S_1) \wedge \neg\text{IsSolvable}(S_5)$ witnesses the exact transition at $n = 5$.
prerequisites: Parts II and III of this file

title: Five Is the Exact Threshold
content:
`five_is_the_threshold` packages the key dichotomy into a single conjunction: `IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin 1)) ∧ ¬IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin 5))`. The Lean proof is a one-line anonymous constructor `⟨s1_solvable, s5_not_solvable⟩` that pairs the two previously established results. This theorem witnesses the sharp transition at n = 5, making the boundary a single quotable, importable result.

The number 5 is not arbitrary — it is the smallest n for which Aₙ is simple and non-abelian. For n ≤ 4, the alternating groups are either trivial (A₁, A₂), cyclic (A₃ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ), or have a non-trivial normal subgroup (A₄ has the Klein four-group V₄ as a normal subgroup). A₅ is the first alternating group with no such escape.

**Bidirectional completion:** The companion gallery entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02` upgrades the threshold witness to a full biconditional: it proves `IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ↔ n ≤ 4` with the forward direction established via explicit derived series constructions for S₂ (`{e} ◁ S₂`), S₃ (`{e} ◁ A₃ ◁ S₃`), and S₄ (`{e} ◁ V₄ ◁ A₄ ◁ S₄`). This makes the solvability classification of all symmetric groups machine-verified: the current file establishes the threshold pair (one solvable, one not), and `oq-04-oq-02` proves it is both necessary and sufficient.
mathContext: $\text{IsSolvable}(S_1) \wedge \neg\text{IsSolvable}(S_5)$. More precisely: $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$, and the transition is sharp at $n = 5$.

title: Part V: The Full Chain in Documentation
content:
Part V shifts from executable Lean code to comprehensive mathematical documentation. While Parts I–IV contain machine-checked theorems, Part V reconstructs the complete 5-step proof chain (including Steps 2, 4, and 5 which are handled internally by Mathlib or require field theory not formalized here) in a structured comment. This serves a dual purpose: it connects the formalized steps to the full mathematical narrative, and it provides degree-by-degree comparison tables that make the 'Why 5?' question visually concrete.

**What Steps 4–5 require:** Step 4 (the Galois bridge) requires Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`, which proves that if a polynomial is solvable by radicals then its splitting field has a solvable Galois group. The underlying mechanism is Kummer theory: each radical extraction creates a cyclic (Kummer) extension, and the tower of such extensions has a solvable Galois group by construction. Step 5 requires showing that the generic polynomial of degree n over ℚ(a₁,...,aₙ) has Galois group Sₙ — this follows from the fact that the elementary symmetric polynomials are algebraically independent (a consequence of Newton's identities and the fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials).
mathContext: The full chain: $A_5$ simple $\Rightarrow$ $A_5$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ $S_n$ ($n \geq 5$) not solvable $\Rightarrow$ solvable Galois group needed $\Rightarrow$ generic quintic unsolvable by radicals.

title: Proof Chain Documentation: Overview and Step 1
content: Part V opens with comprehensive documentation of the full Abel-Ruffini proof chain. The chain begins with Step 1: A₅ is simple and non-abelian, established by Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. This is the only step where the specific structure of A₅ matters — everything else follows by general group-theoretic arguments. The documentation emphasizes three key properties: |A₅| = 60 (the smallest non-abelian simple group), A₅ has no proper non-trivial normal subgroups, and this single fact about A₅ drives the entire impossibility result for the quintic.
mathContext: Step 1: $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian with $|A_5| = 60 = 5!/2$. This is the unique deepest fact in the chain — all subsequent steps are general consequences of simplicity and non-abelianness.

title: Why Simple Non-Abelian Implies Non-Solvable
content:
The core group-theoretic mechanism: for a simple non-abelian group G, the derived subgroup [G,G] is a non-trivial normal subgroup of G. Since G is simple, [G,G] must equal G itself. But solvability requires the derived series G ⊵ [G,G] ⊵ [[G,G],[G,G]] ⊵ ··· to eventually reach {e}. If [G,G] = G, the series is constant: G = G = G = ···, and it never reaches {e}. This is why simplicity is the exact obstruction to solvability.

The Jordan-Hölder theorem provides the deeper structural perspective: the composition factors of a group (the successive quotients in any composition series) are unique up to permutation. For S₅, the composition factors are {ℤ/2ℤ, A₅}. A group is solvable if and only if all its composition factors are cyclic of prime order. Since A₅ is a non-abelian composition factor, S₅ cannot be solvable — and this obstruction is invariant of the choice of composition series.
mathContext: For simple non-abelian $G$: $[G,G] \trianglelefteq G$ is non-trivial (since $G$ is non-abelian), so $[G,G] = G$ (since $G$ is simple). The derived series $G \supseteq [G,G] = G \supseteq \cdots$ never reaches $\{e\}$. By Jordan-Hölder, the composition factors of $S_5$ are $\{\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},\, A_5\}$; solvability requires all factors to be cyclic of prime order.

title: Proof Chain Steps 3–5: From Group Theory to Algebra
content:
Steps 3–5 propagate the non-solvability of A₅ into the impossibility of a radical quintic formula. Step 3 (this file's `symmetric_not_solvable`): Aₙ ◁ Sₙ is normal (kernel of the sign homomorphism), and Aₙ contains A₅ for n ≥ 5 via the natural embedding Fin 5 → Fin n. If Sₙ were solvable, Aₙ would be too (subgroups of solvable groups are solvable), contradicting A₅'s non-solvability. Step 4 (Galois bridge via `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`): radical solvability implies a solvable Galois group, so the contrapositive gives the algebraic impossibility. Step 5 (field theory): the generic quintic x⁵ + a₁x⁴ + ··· + a₅ over ℚ(a₁,...,a₅) has Galois group S₅, which is not solvable by Step 3.

**Kummer theory mechanism (Step 4 detail):** The link 'solvable by radicals ⟹ solvable Galois group' rests on Kummer theory. Each radical extraction α = ⁿ√a adjoins a root of xⁿ − a, creating a Kummer extension K(α)/K whose Galois group embeds into ℤ/nℤ (assuming K contains primitive nth roots of unity — adjoining these first produces an abelian, hence solvable, extension). A radical tower is thus a sequence of cyclic extensions, yielding a subnormal series with cyclic factors: precisely the definition of solvable. The converse (Galois's criterion) is deeper: if Gal(f/K) is solvable, one descends through its composition series, applying Kummer theory at each cyclic quotient to express roots by nested radicals.

**Generalization to differential equations:** The same paradigm extends to differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot theory): a linear ODE is 'solvable by quadratures' (integrals, exponentials, algebraic functions) iff its differential Galois group (a linear algebraic group) has solvable identity component. Kovacic's algorithm (1986) makes this decidable for second-order equations, just as Galois group computation makes radical solvability decidable for polynomials.

**Historical note:** Jordan's *Traité des substitutions* (1870) was the first systematic treatment of permutation groups and established the Jordan-Hölder theorem on uniqueness of composition factors. This theorem is the structural backbone of the entire proof chain: it guarantees that A₅ appearing as a composition factor of S₅ is an intrinsic property, independent of how we decompose S₅. Lagrange's earlier analysis (1770–1771) had shown that the resolvent equation for the quintic has degree 6 rather than the expected degree reduction — a symptom of the non-solvability that Jordan's group-theoretic framework would later explain.
mathContext: Step 3: $A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ with $A_5 \leq A_n$ for $n \geq 5$, so $S_n$ not solvable. Step 4: solvable by radicals $\Rightarrow$ solvable Galois group. Step 5: $\text{Gal}(x^5 + a_1 x^4 + \cdots + a_5 / \mathbb{Q}(a_1,\ldots,a_5)) \cong S_5$. The Jordan-Hölder theorem guarantees these composition factors ($\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and $A_5$) are intrinsic to $S_5$.

title: Why Exactly Degree 5? — Derived Series Table
content:
A summary table showing the derived series for each symmetric group S₁ through S₅, explaining why 5 is the exact threshold. For n ≤ 4, each derived series terminates at {e}: S₂ has one step, S₃ passes through A₃ ≅ ℤ/3ℤ, and S₄ has the longest chain {e} ◁ V₄ ◁ A₄ ◁ S₄. At n = 5, the derived series gets stuck because A₅ is simple: [A₅, A₅] = A₅, so the series A₅ = A₅ = A₅ = ··· never descends. The table crystallizes the insight that A₅ being the first non-abelian simple group (order 60) is the precise algebraic obstruction.

Viewed through the Jordan-Hölder lens: S₄ has composition factors {ℤ/2ℤ, ℤ/3ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ, ℤ/2ℤ} — all cyclic of prime order, hence solvable. S₅ has composition factors {ℤ/2ℤ, A₅} — and A₅ (order 60) is not cyclic of prime order. The transition from S₄ to S₅ is the exact point where a non-cyclic composition factor first appears.
mathContext: Derived series: $S_4$: $\{e\} \triangleleft V_4 \triangleleft A_4 \triangleleft S_4$ (terminates, composition factors $\{\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/3, \mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2\}$). $S_5$: $A_5 = [A_5, A_5]$ is simple, series stuck at $A_5$ (composition factors $\{\mathbb{Z}/2, A_5\}$). The transition $S_4$ solvable $\to$ $S_5$ not solvable is sharp.

title: The Crucial Asymmetry — Degree-by-Degree Radical Solvability
content:
A comparison table showing radical solvability by polynomial degree, from linear through quintic. Degrees 1–4 have explicit radical formulas: the quadratic formula (antiquity), Cardano's cubic formula (1545), and Ferrari's quartic method (1540). At degree 5, the Galois group can be S₅ (which is not solvable), so no general radical formula exists. The table concludes with the crucial distinction: specific quintics like x⁵ - 1 have solvable Galois groups (cyclic, in this case), so the Abel-Ruffini theorem is about the non-existence of a *general* formula, not the unsolvability of every individual quintic.

**Gallery witness for the unsolvable case:** The companion gallery entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01` ("Concrete Abel-Ruffini: Gal(x⁵ - 4x + 2) ≅ S₅ and Unsolvability by Radicals") provides a fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms) concrete example: the polynomial x⁵ - 4x + 2 over ℚ is irreducible by Eisenstein's criterion at p = 2, has exactly three real roots and two complex conjugate roots (from sign analysis of f' = 5x⁴ - 4), and therefore its Galois group is S₅ (a transitive subgroup of S₅ containing a 5-cycle and a transposition must be all of S₅). Since S₅ is not solvable, x⁵ - 4x + 2 cannot be solved by radicals — a concrete instantiation of the general Abel-Ruffini theorem to a specific polynomial. Together, the generic case (this file: S₅ = Gal of generic quintic, not solvable) and the concrete case (oq-04-oq-01: S₅ = Gal(x⁵ - 4x + 2), roots not expressible by radicals) give a complete machine-verified account of quintic unsolvability at both levels.

**Beyond radicals:** The Bring-Jerrard theorem (1786/1834) shows every quintic reduces to the normal form x⁵ + px + q via Tschirnhaus transformations. While this normal form has no solution in the four basic radicals (Abel-Ruffini), it IS solvable using the Bring radical BR(a) — the unique real root of x⁵ + x + a. This shows the impossibility is specifically about the four arithmetic radicals (±, ×, ÷, ⁿ√), not about closed-form expressions in general. Analogously, Hermite (1858) showed quintics are solvable using elliptic modular functions, and Kronecker gave solutions via hypergeometric functions.

**Generic vs. specific bridged by Hilbert irreducibility:** Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (1892) closes a subtle gap in the Abel-Ruffini story. The generic statement says $\text{Gal}(x^5 + a_1 x^4 + \cdots + a_5 / \mathbb{Q}(a_1,\ldots,a_5)) = S_5$ — but this is over the function field $\mathbb{Q}(a_1,\ldots,a_5)$, not over $\mathbb{Q}$ itself. To deduce 'almost every concrete quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ is unsolvable,' one needs that specific rational specializations $a_i = c_i \in \mathbb{Q}$ preserve Galois group $S_5$ for a *dense* set of $(c_1,\ldots,c_5)$. Hilbert's theorem provides exactly this: the set of 'bad' specializations (where the Galois group drops below $S_5$) is *thin* in the Hilbertian sense — has density zero in any natural counting. So for almost all rational coefficient choices, the resulting quintic has $\text{Gal} = S_5$ and hence cannot be solved by radicals. This upgrades Abel-Ruffini from a generic statement to a near-universal one over $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Effective decision procedure:** For any *specific* rational quintic, the Galois group is computable: Stauduhar's algorithm (1973) determines $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ as a transitive subgroup of $S_n$ by computing resolvent polynomials whose factorization patterns distinguish the transitive subgroups (5 transitive subgroups of $S_5$: $C_5, D_5, F_{20}, A_5, S_5$). Modern p-adic refinements (Geißler-Klüners 2000, implemented in Magma and PARI/GP) extend the algorithm to degrees up to 23 and beyond. This converts Abel-Ruffini's negative result into a positive algorithm: given $f \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$, compute $\text{Gal}(f)$, check solvability via the derived series, and either (a) output a radical tower or (b) output a proof that none exists. The unsolvability of *generic* degree-5 polynomials becomes the *decidability* of solvability for *specific* polynomials — a constructive corollary of an a priori non-constructive impossibility theorem.

**Shafarevich completes the constructive side:** For $n \leq 4$, $S_n$ is solvable, and Shafarevich's theorem (1954) guarantees every finite solvable group occurs as $\text{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ for some number field $K$. So the radical formulas of Cardano (cubic) and Ferrari (quartic) are not lucky accidents — they exist because the solvable Galois groups of low-degree polynomials are realizable, and the Galois correspondence translates solvable structure into nested radical extensions. The constructive side (Shafarevich: every solvable group is a Galois group) and the destructive side (Abel-Ruffini: $S_5$ is not solvable) together give a complete picture: degrees 1–4 are solvable because their Galois groups belong to the realizable solvable family; degree 5 fails because $S_5$ exits that family.
mathContext: Degree $n$ solvable by radicals for all polynomials $\iff$ $S_n$ solvable $\iff$ $n \leq 4$. Specific solvable quintics exist: $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 1/\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic, hence solvable.
